claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The proposed PIML surrogate integrates imaging-derived microstructural descriptors with micromechanical simulation outputs.
The PIML model can accurately predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
Local phase composition, grain-size distribution, and interface characteristics can bridge local microstructure and macroscopic mechanical behavior.
Physics-based constraints reduce the overfitting associated with standard machine-learning approaches.
Imaging-derived microstructural features encode the heterogeneities that control the material's mechanical response.
Fusing imaging features with micromechanical outputs enables efficient mapping from local structure to bulk mechanical response.
The proposed fusion reduces dependence on extensive first-principles and CALPHAD computations.
The PIML model will reduce prediction error by at least 20% relative to traditional multiscale simulation approaches.
The PIML model will reduce computational time by approximately a factor of ten.
The method may cease to be reliable when imaging resolution is insufficient to capture key hierarchical features.
The method may cease to be reliable when phase transformations occur outside the training regime.
The method may cease to be reliable when micromechanical simulation inputs are not representative of the material's actual behavior.
The estimated 20% accuracy gain and tenfold efficiency gain are based on early prototype models.
The model's gains may vary with imaging-data quality and simulation fidelity.
Generalizability to samples produced under slightly different processing conditions is uncertain.
A blinded prospective benchmark will compare preregistered model predictions with standardized tensile and fracture-test measurements on independently prepared samples.
The benchmark includes deliberate minor variations in the hierarchical heterostructure.
The stated falsification rule requires both failure to achieve 20% lower error and failure to achieve approximately tenfold computational acceleration.
